desc: The United States Navy is the maritime service of the Department of Defense, organised under a civilian Secretary of the Navy with the Chief of Naval Operations as senior uniformed officer, and it states its purpose as deploying combat-ready sailors, ships, aircraft and submarines worldwide without dependence on foreign land bases. It is the service that generated the modern evidentiary core of the UAP problem: carrier strike group encounters off southern California in November 2004 and off the eastern seaboard in 2014-2015, recorded by F/A-18 targeting pods, SPY-1 radar and aircrew who filed the reports through operational channels. On 27 April 2020 the Department authorised release of three unclassified Navy videos - one from November 2004 and two from January 2015 - and stated on the record that it was doing so to clear up public misconceptions about whether the circulating footage was real. That release is a hinge artifact for this board, because it converts material that had circulated as leak and rumour into acknowledged official product while conspicuously not addressing what the objects were. The Navy also holds the institutional position that matters for custody questions - it operates the fleet ranges where the encounters occurred, the aviation safety and hazard reporting systems into which aircrew reports flow, and the shore facilities repeatedly named in recovery and material-storage allegations elsewhere on this board.

dossier.denialPosture: The board records no denial link on this node in either direction. The posture the record does establish is confirmation without characterisation: the Department confirmed the videos were genuine Navy product and stated in the same release that what they show remains unidentified. The board's own reading of that as damage control rather than disclosure is carried as a Tier 3 inference from the release's wording, and is not treated as a denial by anyone.
dossier.narrative:
The Navy's position on this board is unusual because it is the one institution here that has conceded the evidentiary question in public and declined the interpretive one in the same sentence. The April 2020 release states that the Department was acting 'in order to clear up any misconceptions by the public on whether or not the footage that has been circulating was real, or whether or not there is more to the videos', and in the same document holds that 'The aerial phenomena observed in the videos remain characterized as unidentified.' That is a hinge: material that had circulated as leak became acknowledged official product, and the acknowledgement carried no characterisation with it. The board's own record notes the reading that this was damage control rather than disclosure, and grades that reading Tier 3, because it is an inference from the wording of the release and nothing more.

What gives the service structural weight rather than merely evidentiary weight is what sits under it. The Office of Naval Research was created inside the Office of the Secretary of the Navy with the provision that its orders be considered as emanating from the Secretary and have full force and effect as such. The Deep Submergence Systems Project was assigned by the Secretary to the Special Projects Office and by 1967 was a separate project inside Naval Material Command with its own project designator. The Pais patent names the Secretary of the Navy as the assignee. These are the ordinary mechanics of a service that can commission research, place it under a project office and hold title to what comes out, and they are the mechanics that any custody account of anomalous material would have to run through.

The honest statement of this node is that the board has the outputs and not the interior. Its degree here is nine, its Tier 1 claims number two, and its own research record is a known stub filled in from public description. The Navy is on the map because everything downstream of the 2004 and 2015 encounters passes through it, not because any opened record shows what it did with them.
openQuestions: This node's own research record is a filled stub. It carries four claims, two of them Tier 1, and the board's node letters for consequence, access and disclosure are all zero. A service of this size with this position in the record should not be thinner than its own subordinate offices.

The Navy's aviation safety and hazard reporting systems are the channel every aircrew report entered, and no record of those filings has been opened here. The board asserts the channel exists and holds none of its contents.

Shore facilities under Navy control are repeatedly named in recovery and material-storage allegations elsewhere on this board. Nothing opened for this node names a facility, a programme or a date, and no claim here rests on those allegations.
dossier.whatItIs: The maritime service of the Department of Defense, organised under a civilian Secretary of the Navy with the Chief of Naval Operations as senior uniformed officer, and stating its own purpose as deploying combat-ready sailors, ships, aircraft and submarines worldwide without dependence on foreign land bases. The board holds it through its component parts rather than as a monolith: the Office of Naval Research, placed inside the Office of the Secretary of the Navy by Public Law 79-588 on 1 August 1946; the Deep Submergence Systems Project, assigned by the Secretary to the Special Projects Office after the review group reported in February 1964; the Naval Criminal Investigative Service, a Department of the Navy organisation whose head's title is fixed in the Navy's own codified regulations at 32 CFR part 701; and James V. Forrestal, Secretary of the Navy until September 1947.
dossier.whyImplicated: The Navy generated the modern evidentiary core of the problem this board maps, and then became the office that handled it. The encounters that anchor the contemporary record are Navy carrier aviation events: off southern California in November 2004 and off the eastern seaboard in 2014-2015, recorded through targeting pods and radar and filed by aircrew through operational channels. On 27 April 2020 the Department authorised release of three unclassified Navy videos and said why, and on 4 August 2020 the Deputy Secretary made the Department of the Navy the lead for the UAP Task Force. It is also an assignee of record: the Pais inertial mass reduction device patent is assigned to the United States of America as represented by the Secretary of the Navy. Acknowledgement, custody of the reporting channel and ownership of the exotic-propulsion paperwork are all in the same service.
